item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studi

item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for the student-led, all-campus, annual day of civic celebration! item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: Book Talk — We Shall Outlast Them: Putin’s Global Campaign to Defeat the West
item.description: Stanford Events — How has Russia sustained its confrontation with the West since 2022, and at what cost? In her new book, Hanna Notte argues the Kremlin is waging a war not only on Ukraine but over the global order itself. Notte traces how Russia adapted after the invasion. It worked around sanctions, built new partnerships, cultivated support across the Global South and tried to deepen divisions within Western democracies. Her account combines policy analysis with field reporting from more than a dozen countries and interviews with officials, facilitators and ordinary people drawn into Russia's agenda. The book also examines the domestic consequences. Notte finds that Putin's focus on confronting the West has distorted Russia's economy and moved the country from a tacit dictatorship toward a full one. She suggests Putin may outlast the West, but has gambled Russia's future in the process. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Catherine Johnson - "Mercury’s Enigmatic Magnetic Field"
item.description: Stanford Events — Mercury’s interior structure and its magnetic field are unique among the terrestrial planets and moons of the Solar System. Its large metallic core (~83% of the planetary radius) formed under highly reducing conditions, requiring a core composition that includes substantial silicon and some, but more limited, sulfur and carbon. Mercury is also the only planet other than Earth to have both core and crustal magnetic fields. The core field constrains the present-day dynamo and crustal magnetization, if remanent, can constrain the dynamo history. The core field is dominantly dipolar, axisymmetric, asymmetric about the planetary equator, and ~100 times weaker than Earth’s field at the planetary surface. Structure beyond this simple picture is weak but exists, in particular a high-northern-latitude regional magnetic field anomaly spatially coincident with the topographic and gravity signature of Mercury’s Northern Rise. item.title: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing
item.description: Stanford Events — After the Arab Spring, Tunisia emerged as the one success story to transition to democracy, winning a Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its focus on inclusion and power-sharing. How, then, did its democracy collapse in 2021? Drawing on unique interviews with senior Tunisian officials, alongside three nationally representative surveys of the population, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy points to an overemphasis on compromise, consensus, and power-sharing. Although power-sharing institutions can be useful at the start of a transition, the book finds that extending them beyond that point can lead democracy to unravel by frustrating voters and spurring the rise of populists and extremists. The book takes an in-depth look at Tunisia's transition and then explores how far the theory travels through a quantitative analysis of all democratic transitions between 1942–2020. item.title: Reimagining Democracy: America at 250
item.description: Stanford Events — As part of its free public programming, Stanford Continuing Studies is proud to present the third annual Reimagining Democracy, a weekly speaker series produced with the Office of Community Engagement, the Stanford Democracy Hub, and the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law. This six-part series, hosted by Dean Debra Satz and Professor Larry Diamond, features Stanford scholars who help us understand democracy: how America’s founding 250 years ago shapes public life today, and where we go from here in reimagining and strengthening democratic values and governance, at home and around the world. This year’s series features constitutional, electoral, social science, and humanities experts with conversations connecting to the US November midterm elections and beyond. The series will be recorded and the videos will be available to view at a later date. item.title: Marcela Ibáñez — Authoritarian Aid and Democratic Attitudes: Backlash, Not Diffusion
item.description: Stanford Events — How does the local presence of an authoritarian power shape citizens' commitment to democracy? Existing theories suggest engagement with authoritarian states should weaken democratic commitment through norm diffusion, accommodation, or authoritarian learning. This paper challenges that expectation by examining Chinese development finance in Latin America. Using geocoded data, it estimates the subnational effect of exposure to Chinese aid on democratic attitudes. Exposure increases support for democracy rather than undermining it. The effect is strongest in authoritarian and weakly democratic settings and absent in consolidated democracies. Exposure does not improve perceptions of China or the United States, casting doubt on soft power or foreign-comparison explanations. Instead, the paper argues that visible Chinese projects make incumbents' authoritarian character more salient, triggering an accountability response. item.description: Stanford Events — The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture. We invite you to join us on Thursday, November 5 at 5:30pm PT in the Cedar Room at the Stanford Faculty Club or via livestream for My Cancer Journey: Happiness and Sadness, Hope and Fear. In this talk, Dr. Lin will share a candid and deeply personal reflection on living with terminal cancer. Joining Dr. Lin is Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, a physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice in compassionate, patient-centered care. item.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | Soft Materials for Hard Sustainability Challenges: Water production, Data center Sustainability, and High-Temperature Heat | Carlos Diaz-Marin, Stanford University
item.description: Stanford Events — The Stanford Energy Seminar has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. We aim to bring a wide variety of perspectives to the Stanford community – academics, entrepreneurs, utilities, non-profits, and more. About the talk Water scarcity, rising energy demand, and global emissions are major sustainability challenges of the 21st century. This talk will highlight three soft matter-enabled technologies that the Diaz-Marin lab is developing to tackle these challenges. First, he will present their multiscale design of hydrogel-salt composites to produce water from air in any geography and at costs comparable to those of tap water.
